one_liner: Single-header, zero-allocation C HTTP/1.1 request parser; ~2.26x picohttpparser's scalar build on one sample request, with far less validation.
what_it_does: A ~700-line stb-style header (define HTTPP_IMPLEMENTATION in one TU) that parses an HTTP/1.1 request held in a caller buffer into an httpp_req_t: the method as an int code, and route, version, body and each header name/value as pointer+length spans into that buffer. You supply a fixed-capacity httpp_header_t array (default 20) via httpp_req_init or HTTPP_NEW_REQ, and httpp_parse_request returns the byte offset of the body or -1. It also ships a small response builder (httpp_res_add_header, httpp_res_to_raw) that mallocs the serialized response. The API is its own, not picohttpparser's phr_parse_request.
how_it_is_fast: Zero-copy, zero-allocation parsing: v2.0.0 replaced v1.0.0's per-request malloc/realloc and per-header string copies with spans into the input and a caller-owned stack array, which is why v2 is ~3.1x faster than v1 at -O3 in the project's own table. Field and line boundaries are found with libc memchr (space, CR, ':') and strstr("\r\n") rather than a byte-at-a-time state machine, so scanning runs in glibc's SIMD string routines. It does almost no per-byte validation (no token/CTL tables, no incremental-parse state), so the hot path is delimiter search plus span bookkeeping. There is no hand-written SIMD.
when_to_use: Small or hobby C servers where you control the client or sit behind a validating proxy, and want one dependency-free header with no heap use on the parse path.
The whole request is already in one NUL-terminated buffer, has at most ~20 headers, and you only need route, header and body spans.
Throughput-bound parsing of known-good HTTP/1.1 requests on x86-64/glibc, such as test harnesses, load generators or internal tooling.
You also want a trivial response serializer (status-text table plus header list to a malloc'd raw response) in the same file.
As a short, readable base to fork; the README explicitly invites changes such as replacing the fixed header array with a hash table.
when_not_to_use: Internet-facing servers: no token/CTL validation of the method, route or header names/values, whitespace before ':' is accepted, and duplicate Content-Length headers are not detected, so smuggling and injection defenses are left to you.
Incremental reads from a socket: there is no 'incomplete' result like pico's -2, and a header block cut mid-line returns success with the unterminated tail treated as the body.
Buffers that are not NUL-terminated (raw recv() buffers): header lines are found with strstr, which ignores n and can read past the end of the buffer.

HTTP/1.0 clients, pipelining or chunked bodies: HTTP/1.0 is rejected unless HTTPP_DONT_CHECK_VERSION is defined (then any 8-byte version string passes), the source says pipelined requests are 'not handled well', and chunked decoding is left to the caller.
Production dependencies in general: one maintainer, 9 stars, no issues ever filed, and the latest commit broke the README example and the v2 benchmark, which still call the removed httpp_init_req.

integration.dependencies: none beyond libc (memchr, strstr, strncmp) and POSIX strncasecmp from <strings.h>
integration.min_toolchain: Not documented; the code uses C99 features (designated initializers, compound literals, stdbool) and a commit mentions C11 compatibility. The only compiler named is gcc 15.2.1, in the benchmarks.
integration.platforms: Not documented; portable C with no arch-specific code, but it needs POSIX strncasecmp (MSVC/Windows is not addressed).
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; the parser keeps no global mutable state (everything lives in caller-provided structs), so separate buffers and structs per thread appear safe.

gotchas: Body handling is 'lazy' by default: everything after the blank line is the body. HTTPP_CONSIDER_CONTENT_LENGTH makes it honor Content-Length (it mallocs and atol()s the value), and a Content-Length larger than the remaining buffer returns -1, not 'need more data'.
If there are more headers than the array capacity (default 20), the whole parse returns -1, which you cannot tell apart from a malformed request.
Methods outside the nine built-in ones become HTTPP_METHOD_UNKNOWN, and httpp_req_t has no method span, so the text of methods such as PROPFIND is lost. Methods over 10 bytes are rejected.

Spans are not NUL-terminated and point into your buffer, so the buffer must outlive the request; httpp_span_to_str returns a malloc'd copy. httpp_res_to_raw prints headers with %s, so response header strings must be NUL-terminated. The implementation also leaks unprefixed macros (LTRIM, RTRIM, SETSTR) and reserved __-prefixed names into the translation unit that defines HTTPP_IMPLEMENTATION.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick httpp only for a tiny self-contained C header with a response builder when the input is known to be complete, well-formed and NUL-terminated; for a speedup that keeps pico's API, validation and -2 incremental parsing, the vkrasnov AVX2 fork (1.68-1.79x) is safer, picohttpparser-rs covers Rust, and hparse reports a smaller ~12.5% wall-time gain but ~4x fewer instructions than pico.
verified_claims_summary: This is the project's own benchmark: 10M parses x 5 runs of picohttpparser's classic 9-header 'hello-kitty' GET, timed with clock() and built with gcc 15.2.1 -O3 and no -march on an unspecified 'Ryzen 7' (4.79 GHz peak). httpp 2.0.0 took 1.12 s (~8.9M req/s) against picohttpparser's 2.54 s (~3.9M req/s), about 2.26x, while httpp 1.0.0 was slower than pico. Pico was built without -msse4.2, so its SSE4.2 path was off; it was cloned unpinned and built as a separate TU, and an earlier README run on the same stated hardware had pico at 4.91M req/s, a 1.83x ratio.
status_note: The record says active, but the last commit was 2025-12-21, about 9 months ago (33 commits from one author since 2025-11-18). It is MIT-licensed and small enough (~730 lines) to vendor and audit; vendor the 2.0.0 release asset, since the init functions were renamed after it.
